story.hook: My Landlord Charged Me for His Leak
story.script: The first warning was my water bill. It had nearly tripled even though I lived alone, took quick showers, and had spent one week visiting my parents. I checked every tap, photographed the meter, and sent the bill to my landlord. He replied within five minutes saying higher prices were normal and I should learn to conserve water. The next morning, I noticed the meter was still moving while every tap and appliance in my apartment was off. I recorded a ten-minute video showing the numbers climbing and sent that too. He said meters sometimes moved by themselves and told me not to create unnecessary maintenance work. Two days later, a damp patch appeared above my kitchen window. It spread across the ceiling each night, then partly dried during the afternoon. My landlord finally visited, looked at it from the doorway, and decided the problem was condensation from my cooking. I reminded him that I had not cooked all week because the kitchen smelled like wet plaster. He handed me a printed notice claiming I had caused moisture damage through improper ventilation. The notice demanded six hundred dollars for inspection and repainting, payable with the next rent. It also warned that refusing could affect my deposit. I did not argue. I asked him to sign and date the notice, and he did. Then I emailed the building management office with the meter video, the water bills, the ceiling photographs, and his signed demand. Management sent their own licensed plumber the following morning. The plumber shut every valve inside my apartment, but the meter kept spinning. He followed the pipe through a service cupboard in the corridor and found a second line branching off after my meter. That line ran upstairs to a storage tank supplying the landlord's rooftop garden and automatic irrigation system. A cracked connector beside the tank had been leaking day and night. The water soaking my ceiling and the water feeding his garden had both been billed to my apartment. The plumber estimated the arrangement had existed since before I moved in. Management pulled the previous year's utility readings and found the same unexplained pattern under the former tenant. The old maintenance log even contained two complaints about damp plaster in exactly the same place. Both had been closed after my landlord called them cooking moisture. I added copies of those records to the folder with his signed demand because his explanation was becoming more expensive by the minute. Building management asked my landlord to attend immediately. He arrived smiling until the plumber showed him the branch line and explained that it crossed common property without approval. My landlord stopped discussing condensation. He tried to call the extra pipe an old emergency connection, but management had renovation records showing that he installed the rooftop garden only three years earlier. They ordered him to isolate the line, repair the ceiling, reimburse my excess water charges, and provide documentation for every modification he had made. They also told him his six-hundred-dollar damage notice had no basis. He withdrew it that afternoon, but I replied that I would keep the signed copy for my records. The final calculation covered six months of inflated bills, the plumber's investigation, and temporary accommodation while the damaged ceiling was opened and dried. My landlord owed me more than four times the amount he had demanded. He asked whether we could settle privately if I stopped communicating through building management. I said written records had suddenly become very important to me. For the rest of my lease, every repair request was answered promptly, every bill was itemized, and the rooftop garden was watered through a properly approved meter. The damp patch disappeared, my water bill returned to normal, and the only thing that kept leaking was my landlord's confidence whenever he saw me taking another photograph.
